Only manual Update or a missing payload starts a download.

Result: 'M5-update-listDue-expiry SURVIVED ok | 742 passed | 0 failed | 7 ignored'. The run left out privacy-generic, privacy-mask and vendor-pin (they need .git or docs/). grep showed these 3 files do not reference listDue. Repro docs/review-2026-11-16/repros/listdue-expiry.test.js output: original {fetched:8}, mutant {fetched:0}. Call site: update.js:868 'if (!listDue(meta, now, manual, !!meta)) continue;'. Not checked: behavior in a real Chrome.

verdict.reason: Confirmed. In a scratch copy (docs/review-2026-11-16/repros/verify-tests-quality/r1) I changed the last line of listDue (update.js:637) to 'return false;'. I then ran the 21 test files that call refresh or reference the alarm, with --parallel: 206 passed, 0 failed. The reviewer's full-suite run also survived. The only tests that seed expiresMs (final-lists-2, no-openphish) use manual:true or applyEnabled, so the expiry branch of an automatic refresh never runs in a test. Thus a regression that stops the 3 h alarm from refetching expired lists would go out unnoticed. Lists would then stay at their first download until a manual Update.
verdict.why_it_may_be_intentional: None found. The comment above listDue explains the design (manual refreshes are conditional, and a missing payload is always refetched). Nothing says that the expiry branch is left untested on purpose.

Run U.refresh(deps, {manual:false}) at now = T + 10 days. Assert that every source is fetched. Then seed fetchedAt = now - 1 h (not expired), with lastRunAt older than MIN_INTERVAL_MS, and assert that no source is fetched. confirmed.failure_scenario: An upstream update changes processM3U8 so that stitched-ad segments are kept. The update script writes a new pin, and the string tests are edited to match. The suite passes. No test runs the code on a real ad playlist. CHANGELOG says the player could not be tested live.
confirmed.evidence: Checked in this session: grep of test/ for each fixture name. The m3u8 fixtures appear only in test/fixtures.test.js. I read swap.test.js in full and page.test.js lines 7-72 (all source.includes / block.includes). I read vendor-pin.test.js:23 and scripts/vendor-pins.json. Not checked: whether processM3U8 can run in Deno with small stubs (the code is built into a worker blob string).
confirmed.suggested_fix: Do not change the frozen vendor file. Add a harness that evals processM3U8 + stripAdSegments from the vendor source with stub globals. Run them on the 4 m3u8 fixtures and assert on output segments. Remove the string tests that the SHA pin already covers, or merge them into one 'pin' test.

verdict.reason: Partly confirmed. fixtures.test.js imports the 4 m3u8 fixtures and checks only marker strings. No test runs processM3U8 or stripAdSegments (grep shows only source-string checks in swap, page and bug tests). vendor-pin.test.js:23 pins the vendored file by SHA-256 and size, so while the pin holds, the string checks add almost nothing. But the vendored file is frozen upstream code (the release gate, and CHANGELOG line 63 says the player could not be tested live). Thus the practical risk is only at a vendor update, and the impact is low.
verdict.why_it_may_be_intentional: The vendor file is frozen and upstream-owned. The string tests were probably written before the SHA pin existed (scripts/vendor-pins.json and the update script came later). They document which upstream behaviors the project depends on, so a vendor update shows a readable diff of what changed.
verdict.fix_notes: Do not change src/vendor/video-swap-new.user.js. Add test/twitch-playlist.test.js. Get the source of function stripAdSegments and function processM3U8 from the vendor text (the same indexOf slices that swap.test.js uses), and eval them with stub globals (AD_SIGNIFIER, a streamInfo object, a realFetch stub). Run stripAdSegments on twitch-stitched-ad.m3u8 and twitch-maf-ad.m3u8, and assert that the ad segments are removed or blanked and the live segments stay. After that, the owner can merge the string tests that the SHA pin covers into one 'upstream behaviors we depend on' test.

confirmed.description: looksLikeDomain uses localAddress to reject non-public IPv4 literals in filter lists. A mutant that removes the '(a === 100 && b >= 64 && b <= 127)' term survives the suite. The same term in threat/protected-hosts.js:72 is covered (mutant M8 killed).
confirmed.failure_scenario: A refreshed list holds '0.0.0.0 100.64.1.1' or '||100.64.1.1^'. With the mutant, it becomes a whole-domain block entry. No test fails.
confirmed.evidence: Checked in this session: 'M4-update-localAddress-cgnat SURVIVED ok | 742 passed' in docs/review-2026-11-16/repros/repo (3 git/docs files left out; they do not reference localAddress). 'M8-protected-cgnat KILLED'. Not checked: what Chrome does with an IP literal in requestDomains (UNVERIFIED).
confirmed.suggested_fix: Add a case to the parseEntries tests: 100.64.0.1 and 100.127.255.255 are rejected, 100.63.0.1 (privacy-check: allow) and 100.128.0.1 (privacy-check: allow) are kept. Better: let update.js and protected-hosts.js share one local-address function.

verdict.reason: Confirmed. In the scratch copy I removed '|| (a === 100 && b >= 64 && b <= 127)' from update.js localAddress (line 174). I then ran the 13 test files that reference parseList, looksLikeDomain, IP literals or private ranges (privacy-generic was left out because it needs .github): 108 passed, 0 failed. psl.test.js:51 tests 100.64.0.1 only for the PSL or protected-hosts copy, not for update.js. The impact is low: CGNAT literals rarely appear in public lists, and a block on one would affect only that IP.
verdict.why_it_may_be_intentional: None. The same range in threat/protected-hosts.js is covered, and the two copies are separate on purpose (worker vs threat module), but nothing documents that the update.js copy is left untested on purpose.
verdict.fix_notes: In the list-refresh (parse) tests, assert that U.parseList (or the exported entry parser) rejects '0.0.0.0 100.64.0.1', '||100.127.255.255^' and '||100.64.1.1^', and keeps 100.63.255.255 (privacy-check: allow) and 100.128.0.1 (privacy-check: allow). Optionally make update.js reuse GeckoPsl or protected-hosts localAddress, so that there is one copy. If update.js does not export localAddress, test it through parseList.

confirmed.title: The suite is about 4x faster with --parallel, but CI and the release gate run it serially
confirmed.description: The baseline full run takes about 5 minutes serially. In the scratch copy, the same 742 tests passed in 1m18s-1m23s with 'deno test --parallel' (3 git/docs files left out), with no failures in 6 runs. Many files build 30,000-domain synthetic lists (grep: 13 files), which costs time.
confirmed.failure_scenario: Each push and each release-gate run waits about 5 minutes for tests that can finish in about 1.5 minutes.
confirmed.evidence: Checked in this session: 6 mutation-survivor or baseline runs with --parallel in docs/review-2026-11-16/repros/repo gave 'ok | 742 passed | 0 failed' in 78-83 s. Not checked: --parallel on the real checkout with .git, on Windows, or in GitHub Actions; timing-based tests (race.test.js:146 waits 600 ms; dnr-queue uses tick(150)) may be flaky under load.

verdict.reason: Partly confirmed. checks.yml:46 and release-gate.sh:739 both run 'deno test' without --parallel. My own --parallel runs in the scratch copy (206 tests in 1m24s, 108 tests in 23s) passed. No test is run with --allow-write, so tests cannot share written files, and that lowers the risk of parallel races. This is an efficiency improvement, not a correctness defect. Flakiness on 4-vCPU GitHub runners and on Windows is UNVERIFIED.
verdict.why_it_may_be_intentional: Nothing documents why the runs are serial. Timing tests (race.test.js waits 600 ms, dnr-queue tick(150)) may be the reason, and running serially keeps the failure output in order for the release-gate summary parse (it reads /tmp/gate-deno.txt).
verdict.fix_notes: In .github/workflows/checks.yml 'Run tests', add --parallel, and check over 5-10 CI runs that no test is flaky. Make the release gate parallel only after that. Check that the gate's summary parse still finds the 'ok | N passed' line with --parallel output. Optionally cache one 30,000-domain synthetic list in test/fixtures.

rejected.title: A '~host' exclusion on a generic hide rule also removes a site rule for a subdomain of that host
rejected.reason: The mechanism is real by code reading. hiddenElsewhere (cosmetic-parse.js:314-318) and mergeCosmetic hiddenByOther (380-381) look only at candidateHosts(h), which are h and its parents. buildPageCss (449-465) applies the exceptions of all candidate hosts to the site selectors too (cssForSelectors(siteSels, exc)). Thus '~a.com##.x' together with 'shop.a.com##.x' removes .x on shop.a.com. But the reporter's own scan finds 0 such pairs in today's EasyList and EasyPrivacy. AdGuard Base is sites-only, so generic '~host' rules from it are dropped. The impact today is nil, so this is a latent edge case, not a confirmed defect. NOT CHECKED in this session: the reporter's repro (I could not run Bash).

rejected.title: Hooked fetch throws synchronously for a Request whose body was already used (native fetch returns a rejected promise)
rejected.reason: The repro output is right (hooks.mjs: 'hooked fetch threw synchronously: TypeError: Body is unusable'), but the path is unreachable in the shipped configuration. The hooks are installed only when HOOKS = !uboLayerPresent() || OPTS.hooksUnderUbo (youtube.js:1129). Each call also stands down to native through cloak()/hooksLive() once the marker is present (youtube.js:1131-1138, 1172-1180). The uBO bundle runs first in the manifest on the same hosts (manifest.json:73-82 and :102-111). It sets the marker without a condition at the end (src/vendor/ubo-youtube.js:2017), and each scriptlet is wrapped in try. The youtubeScriptlets feature is 'apply: always' and cannot be switched off (src/settings/features.js:46, owner decision D-3). So production YouTube pages never call this fetch hook. The detection probe also needs a page that deliberately feeds fetch a Request whose body was already used.

rejected.title: Stripped youtubei Response loses url, redirected and type (uBO's own prune keeps them)
rejected.reason: The repro output is right (url='' type=default on a stripped response), but it is on the same fail-open hook path as #3, and that path is not reachable in the shipped configuration (the marker is always set by src/vendor/ubo-youtube.js:2017, youtubeScriptlets is always on according to features.js:46, and hooks stand down at youtube.js:1129/1177). YouTube's player code does not read resp.url, as far as anything in the repository shows. So the impact is negligible.

rejected.title: XHR 'json' response getter returns a new deep copy on every read
rejected.reason: The repro output is right (xhr.response === xhr.response is false). The json branch at youtube.js:1891-1897 has no cache, but the text path does (stripXhrText, youtube.js:1851-1866). However, the getter is installed only on the HOOKS path (fail-open, no uBO marker), and that path is unreachable in the shipped configuration for the same reasons as #3. The impact in production is nil.

rejected.title: Decoy detection depends on the local clock: a PC clock about 31 h fast or 7 days slow marks every real stream URL as a decoy
rejected.reason: The math is right (clock.mjs: true at +31 h and at -168 h). But the effect in the shipped configuration is negligible. Under uBO, isDecoyStreamUrl is used only by the read-only PerformanceObserver (youtube.js:1157), which sets uboDecoyThisNav. That flag only shortens the gentle watchdog wait (decoyFast, youtube.js:1469), and only while nothing is buffered and the player is not moving (playerMoving stops the watchdog at readyState >= 2). A healthy start is never reloaded because of this. The path that reloads at once on decoys (onDecoyUrl from the fetch hook) is the fail-open hook path, and that path is unreachable when the uBO marker is present (see #3). A PC clock that is more than 30 h wrong also breaks other things on YouTube and Google (cookies, sign-in), so this is an edge case.

rejected.title: Kill latch is released by any extension version change, also when the stolen key is still pinned
rejected.reason: This is the documented behavior. docs/feed-setup.md 'Emergency switches' says the latch lasts 'until the extension itself is updated (ship new pinned keys in that update if the feed key was stolen)'. The owner controls every release, so an update that ships with the old pinned key is a procedure error, not a code defect. The proposed safeguard (release the latch only when the pinned keys change) is a reasonable hardening, but the current design is intended and documented.

rejected.title: Kill document has no time check: any old (or future-dated) kill document latches fresh installs
rejected.reason: The repro (test E) confirms that a kill document with an old or a future createdAt is accepted on a fresh install. But the attacker in this scenario already controls the feed host, so the attacker can already deny the feed by serving nothing or garbage. A replayed kill only switches the feed off until the next version (the kill key can only switch off). The packed threat tier and public lists keep running (docs 'Emergency switches'). The extra harm is negligible.

rejected.title: Packed threat ruleset blocks whole first-party service hosts of large providers (Daum Mail attachments, Huawei Cloud mirror, vendor download CDNs)
rejected.reason: The hosts are in the packed set: attach.mail.daum.net, repo.huaweicloud.com, cdn.gomlab.com, softdl.360tpcdn.com and cfs7.blog.daum.net are all in requestDomains of src/rules/threat-network.json. But they are there because the curated upstream list names them as hosts that currently serve malware ('online' list). attach.mail.daum.net is also blocked as a whole domain, independently, by HaGeZi (lists/hagezi.txt:17228), so the ordinary tier blocks it too. The extension's documented model is to trust these curated lists. The proposed 'shared service host' deny list is a policy addition, not a correction of a defect. No user-visible false positive was shown: the reviewer marked what each host serves as UNVERIFIED. The user remedy (Settings -> Allow this domain) exists and is documented.

rejected.title: Static 'threat' ruleset is a permanent floor: hosts removed upstream stay blocked until the next extension release
rejected.reason: The behaviour is real: setThreatRuleset() runs only on a switch change (general-background.js:318-332), and applyThreatRules never disables the static 'threat' ruleset. A host delisted upstream therefore stays blocked until the next release. But this is the documented design: update.js:550 says 'the static "threat" ruleset stays the floor', and update.js:1267 says 'the packed `threat` ruleset is the floor'. The CHANGELOG shows the same choice made on purpose for the general ruleset. The impact is small: 25 of 15,865 hosts after two days, most of them still-malicious or tunnel hosts. 'Allow this domain' removes any real false positive. The proposed fix trades away offline and partial-refresh resilience: a missing or held list, or a refresh that fails while the static set is disabled, would drop protection.

rejected.title: IDN hosts are shown only in punycode in the popup and settings lists
rejected.reason: The behavior is correct, but the impact is negligible, and showing punycode is a known protective choice. The stored key is right and the save works. Chrome itself shows punycode for many IDNs (its homograph policy), so the Unicode form in the address bar is not guaranteed. A decoder in the popup could also show a lookalike name and make spoofing easier. This is a UX preference and not a defect.

rejected.title: Gate section 4 'scoped extension API' check misses packaged worker files and common call forms
rejected.reason: The gaps exist. The five worker/general files are not in any section 4 list, and the regex misses chrome?.x, chrome['x'] and destructuring. But none of these files uses chrome.* today, so this is a latent gap only. Also, the real API boundary is the manifest permission set, which section 2 enforces strictly (storage, declarativeNetRequest, alarms). A chrome.scripting or chrome.webRequest call fails at runtime without the permission. chrome.tabs.query without the 'tabs' permission gives no URLs. Page-world scripts have no chrome.* at all. A missed call in an unlisted file therefore cannot gain new privilege, so the impact is negligible.

rejected.title: STORE-REVIEW-NOTES does not cover the vendored Twitch script's handling of the user's Authorization token and the code it builds from a string
rejected.reason: Not a defect. docs/permissions-and-privacy.md:48 already discloses that the Twitch script copies the page's Authorization and Client-Integrity headers and sends them only to Twitch. The token never leaves the page to the developer or to any server of ours. The blob worker is built from strings in the package plus Twitch's own worker source, which is not remote code under MV3 rules. What a store reviewer or the privacy form would conclude is speculation. Nothing has been submitted (TODO.md:40). At most this is a helpful addition to STORE-REVIEW-NOTES.md, not a confirmed problem.

rejected.title: Test DNR matcher uses the last two labels as the site for domainType, and matches regexFilter with case
rejected.reason: The header of test/fixtures/dnr-matcher.js:12 documents 'site = last two labels' as a deliberate simplification. The reviewer and I found no current test that uses a multi-label public suffix with domainType, or a mixed-case regexFilter. No test asserts a wrong result today, and the Chrome behavior is UNVERIFIED. The finding is a latent limit of the oracle, so I rate it speculation, not a defect.

rejected.title: 11.2 MB of byte-identical, unreferenced images in docs/
rejected.reason: The folders are identical: diff -rq of docs/cards against cards2 and cards-main shows no difference, and I found no reference to them in the repository. But TODO.md:41 already lists 'Tidy docs/ ... the many cards-* folders could move to an archive folder or be removed'. The files are not in the extension zip, so users are not affected. Git history keeps the blobs, so a clone does not get smaller. The impact is negligible and the item is already known.

rejected.title: A known-issue test is ignored with 'ignore: true', so it never reports a fix or a further regression
rejected.reason: The ignored test is a documented, deliberate known-issue marker. The comment at lines 94-98 explains why it is not fixed in 0.3.5: it needs DNR allow rules or split parent blocks, which is too risky for this release. TODO.md:9 counts it among the '6 owner-decision or known-issue tests'. Changing it to an expected-known test only adds change detection for a known upstream-list effect. The impact is negligible.
